title: The Family Reunion as Cultural Infrastructure
question: What social and historical functions does the reunion perform?

claims.claim: Black family reunions are recurring, family-governed institutions with formal organizational structures: dues, registration fees, committees, written by-laws, minutes, bank accounts, and rotating host families.
claims.source: Allen Family Reunion meeting minutes (PDF, 2016); Ebony, 'How to plan a family reunion you will never forget' (1993); Copeland, 'Ensuring the Continuity of the African-American Family Reunion by Organizing a Nonprofit Entity,' Western Journal of Black Studies (2018)
claims.source_type: Primary artifact (minutes); contemporary practice journalism; peer-reviewed legal/sociological article
claims.evidence: 2016 minutes document a bank account and balance, $180 annual dues, named scholarship recipients, a $500 scholarship donation, and a family-history report. The 1993 Ebony planning article lists standing committees (scholarship, by-laws, church, social, reclamation), dues/registration fees, and host-family logistics. Copeland (2018) documents recurring host groups, limited capital, and weak recordkeeping/accounting as typical organizational problems.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None located; Copeland notes many reunions are informally run, which qualifies but does not contradict formalization where it occurs.
claims.notes: Functional claims held to strictest grading; VERIFIED because three independent sources (one a primary artifact) converge on governance structures.

claims.claim: Reunions transmit lineage and family history through elders, formal presentations, genealogy research, photographs, video, books, and printed programs.
claims.source: NNPA/AFRO op-ed, 'The Legacy of Family Reunions' (Jasmine Clarke, 2024); Allen Family Reunion minutes (2016); Ebony planning article (1993)
claims.source_type: Journalism (op-ed with archival detail); primary artifact; contemporary practice journalism
claims.evidence: Thelma Doswell's family trees (1,500 names in 1959; 5,000+ names in 1991) were built from reunion-centered genealogical work and are held by LOC, the Reginald F. Lewis Museum, and the Virginia Museum of History and Culture. The 2016 minutes include a family-history report and Ancestry.com research. The 1993 Ebony article documents lineage presentations, photograph collection, videotaping, and family history books as standard reunion activities.
claims.notes: Convergence across a primary artifact, a case history, and practice journalism.

claims.claim: Reunions coordinate money: annual dues, registration fees, scholarship funds, and donations.
claims.source: Allen Family Reunion minutes (2016); Ebony planning article (1993)
claims.evidence: 2016 minutes: $180 annual dues, named scholarship recipients, $500 scholarship donation, bank balance. 1993 Ebony: dues/registration fees; family associations/corporations described as offering loans, advice, and scholarships.
claims.notes: Direct documentary evidence of financial coordination.

claims.claim: Some reunions formalize as nonprofit entities or family associations/corporations; organizers report limited capital and weak recordkeeping as persistent problems.
claims.source: Copeland (2018); Ebony planning article (1993)
claims.source_type: Peer-reviewed article (partly normative/legal argument); contemporary practice journalism
claims.evidence: Copeland documents recurring host groups, limited capital, weak recordkeeping/accounting, and argues for nonprofit incorporation to ensure continuity. Ebony (1993) describes family associations/corporations offering loans, advice, and scholarships.
claims.notes: Copeland is partly prescriptive; claims about what reunions 'typically' do are qualified rather than taken as representative.

claims.claim: Reunions recognize elders and socialize younger members (elder tributes, youth activities, scholarships).
claims.source: Ebony planning article (1993); Temple University memorial for Ione Vargus (2026); Allen Family Reunion minutes (2016)
claims.source_type: Practice journalism; institutional memorial; primary artifact
claims.evidence: Ebony (1993) lists elder tributes and youth activities among standard program elements. Temple's memorial notes Vargus's emphasis on youth in reunion research. The 2016 minutes document scholarships to younger members.
claims.notes: Consistent across sources but program details vary by family; not universal.

claims.claim: Returning to Southern places of origin (old homestead, hometowns) is a documented reunion practice and prescription.
claims.source: Ebony planning article (1993); Jones (1980) via secondary summary; Temple memorial for Vargus (2026); NNPA op-ed (2024)
claims.source_type: Practice journalism; peer-reviewed anthropology (via secondary summary); institutional memorial; op-ed
claims.evidence: Ebony (1993) quotes Chicago writer Dee Parmer Woodtoor arguing reunions should be held where the family originated, and documents return-to-the-South/old-homestead practice. Jones (1980) studied Black homecomings in a North Carolina county. Vargus followed migration routes north to Boston and south to the Carolinas in reunion fieldwork. NNPA (2024) quotes an attendee on reunions taking families 'back to hometowns.'
claims.notes: Practice and prescription both documented; frequency and Chicago-specificity not established (see C007).

claims.claim: Many Black Chicago families hold reunions in Southern hometowns (documented reverse-migration reunion pattern).
claims.source: None located
claims.evidence: No Chicago-specific archival, newspaper, or oral-history evidence located in this research pass. The 1993 Ebony article gives a Chicago-area host example (Lansing, IL) and quotes a Chicago writer, but does not document Chicago-to-South reunion travel specifically. Chicago Defender searches did not yield reunion notices in accessible sources.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None located; absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.
claims.notes: Major gap. Likely sources: ProQuest Historical Newspapers/Chicago Defender, Chicago Public Library Vivian G. Harsh Collection, Abbott-Sengstacke papers. Flagged as priority follow-up.

claims.claim: In a North Carolina county, homecomings symbolized obligations to kin and community, restored connection between the living and the dead, and enabled multigenerational transmission; a documented 1937 Gorgus, NC homecoming was familial rather than church-sponsored.
claims.source: Jones, 'Kinship Affiliation through Time: Black Homecomings and Family Reunions in a North Carolina County,' Ethnohistory 27 (1980), via secondary cultural-resource summary
claims.source_type: Peer-reviewed anthropology (via secondary summary; original not inspected)
claims.evidence: A secondary cultural-resource summary attributes these functional findings to Jones and reports the 1937 Gorgus homecoming as familial rather than church-sponsored.
claims.notes: PROVISIONAL until the original article (DOI 10.2307/481627) is obtained and inspected. Functional claims require the strictest grading.

claims.claim: Ione D. Vargus conducted participant-observation and in-depth interviews at 14 reunions (summer 1986), founded the African American Family Reunion Conference (1988) and Temple University's Family Reunion Institute (1990), and authored Black Family Reunions: Finding the Rest of Me (2020).
claims.source: Temple University news (2011); Temple University memorial (2026)
claims.evidence: Temple (2011) reports 14 reunions studied in summer 1986, the 1988 conference, and the 1990 Institute. Temple (2026) memorial confirms the book and describes her treatment of the reunion as an independently Black-controlled institution.
claims.notes: Institutional sources have memorial framing; factual claims (dates, counts) are straightforward.

claims.claim: At a 2001 Atlanta-area Thompson family reunion, participants recalled slavery, Jim Crow, the Great Migration, poverty, Klan violence, and later professional and family achievements.
claims.source: Auslander, 'Something We Need to Get Back To': Mythologies of Origin and Rituals of Solidarity in African American Working Families,' Emory Center for Myth and Ritual in American Life Working Paper No. 6 (2001)
claims.evidence: Working paper abstract reports fieldwork at the 2001 reunion and the range of historical memory participants invoked.
claims.notes: Based on abstract; full paper (core.ac.uk/display/100140297) not yet retrieved. Single-family case; not generalizable.

claims.claim: Black family reunions involve technical-communication literacies: the writing and rhetorical practices of planning, programs, newsletters, and online coordination.
claims.source: Allen, 'Handling Family Business: Technical Communication Literacies in Black Family Reunions,' Technical Communication Quarterly 31(3) (2022); Allen dissertation, Hospitable Literacies (2020), via lauralallen.com
claims.source_type: Peer-reviewed article (topic/scope verified); author research page
claims.evidence: Article title, journal, and award verified; author's site confirms the 2020 dissertation on the writing and rhetorical practices of Black family reunions online and offline.
claims.notes: Topic and existence verified; specific findings not yet read from full text. Graded on scope only.

claims.claim: Reunions produce and circulate material culture: T-shirts, banners, mugs, family emblems, history books, souvenir programs; videotaping and professional photography are standard.
claims.source: Ebony planning article (1993); Ebony, 'Black America's multimillion-dollar reunion season' (2004)
claims.evidence: Ebony (1993): sales of family emblems, T-shirts, mugs, banners, history books; videotaping and professional photography. Ebony (2004): T-shirts among businesses serving the reunion market.
claims.notes: Advice/market journalism, not a representative survey; items vary by family.

claims.claim: Reunion season generates measurable tourism spending: the Greenville-Pitt County (NC) visitors bureau estimated $2.3 million annually from Black reunions; Chicago is among cities courting reunion business. (A cited $428 average friends/relatives leisure-trip spend is not reunion-specific.)
claims.source: Ebony, 'Black America's multimillion-dollar reunion season' (2004)
claims.evidence: Article documents reunion spending categories and tourism-industry targeting, cites the Greenville-Pitt County estimate and Chicago among courting cities; the $428 figure is explicitly for friends/relatives leisure trips excluding transportation, not reunions.
claims.notes: Dated (2004); the $2.3M figure is a local bureau estimate; no national reunion-spending total documented. Use with caveats.

claims.claim: Thelma Doswell's family trees: her 1959 tree measured 8 x 6 feet with 1,500 names; her 1991 tree held over 5,000 names; the trees are held by the Library of Congress, the Reginald F. Lewis Museum, and the Virginia Museum of History and Culture.
claims.source: NNPA/AFRO op-ed, 'The Legacy of Family Reunions' (Jasmine Clarke, 2024)
claims.evidence: Op-ed reports tree dimensions, name counts, and the three institutional holders; Doswell is documented as a reunion genealogist from the Felix/Blackwell family of Virginia.
claims.notes: Single source; institutional holdings not independently verified at LOC/Lewis/VMHC. Do not generalize one family's archive to all reunions.

claims.claim: The Felix/Blackwell family reunion began in 1953, following the 1952 funeral of family matriarch Nay Woodrow Blackwell; genealogist Thelma Doswell descends from Melbahu Gibbs.
claims.source: NNPA/AFRO op-ed, 'The Legacy of Family Reunions' (Jasmine Clarke, 2024)
claims.evidence: Op-ed traces the reunion's origin to the 1952 funeral and first gathering in 1953, with Doswell's lineage noted.
claims.notes: Single journalistic source; presented as this family's documented history, not as the first reunion ever.

claims.claim: Women perform central genealogical and organizing labor in reunions (e.g., Thelma Doswell, Melbahu Gibbs, quoted planners Doris Saunders and Myranda Strickland); systematic gender data on reunion organizing is absent.
claims.source: NNPA op-ed (2024); Ebony planning article (1993)
claims.evidence: Doswell and Gibbs documented as the Blackwell family's genealogists; Saunders and Strickland quoted as reunion planning authorities in Ebony (1993).
claims.notes: Case-level evidence is consistent; no quantitative gender breakdown of organizers located. Do not state 'mostly women' as a verified general fact.

claims.claim: The NCNW Black Family Reunion Celebration (conceived by Dorothy Height; first held on the National Mall, September 1986) is a public, organization-sponsored cultural festival — distinct from kin-governed family reunions.
claims.source: AAIHS, 'Dorothy Height, NCNW, and the National Black Family Reunion'; Congressional Record (2004 tribute to Height)
claims.evidence: AAIHS documents the first two-day event (second weekend of September 1986, National Mall) with booths, health screenings, vendors, and concerts; the Congressional Record confirms Height conceived and organized the Celebration in 1986. The Cincinnati/Midwest regional began in 1989.
claims.notes: Boundary definition rests on governance: NCNW-sponsored public festival vs. family-governed kin institution.

claims.claim: NMAAHC's Robert Frederick Smith Explore Your Family History Center has guided more than 25,000 visitors through genealogy research sessions and hosted more than 100 virtual and in-person programs since 2017; its Community Curation Platform collects personal and community histories.
claims.source: NMAAHC, 'Family History Research for Your Family Reunion' (event page)
claims.evidence: Museum's own program page states the 25,000-visitor and 100-program figures and describes the Community Curation Platform.
claims.notes: Institutional self-report; figures are program outputs, not reunion-function evidence.

claims.claim: Church homecomings and family reunions are distinct institutions: Jones (1980) documented a familial homecoming in Gorgus, NC that was not church-sponsored.
claims.source: Jones (1980), via secondary cultural-resource summary
claims.source_type: Peer-reviewed anthropology (via secondary summary; original not inspected)
claims.evidence: Secondary summary reports the 1937 Gorgus homecoming as familial rather than church-sponsored.
claims.notes: PROVISIONAL until the original article is inspected. Boundary analytic (governance-based) is the brief's own framework.

claims.claim: Reunion materials enter institutional archives: Alexandria Library's Local History/Special Collections runs a 'Black Family Reunion' scanning project; NMAAHC's collection holds a Perryman family reunion photograph (Gift of Eddie Faye Gates).
claims.source: WUSA9 news segment, ''Black Family Reunion' aims to fill gaps in documented history of Alexandria's black families' (YouTube); NMAAHC event page (2022)
claims.source_type: News video (description verified via oEmbed); institutional page
claims.evidence: Video description: Alexandria's Black residents asked to bring family documents/images to be scanned into the Library's archive. NMAAHC page: feature image 'Perryman family reunion,' Collection of NMAAHC, Gift of Eddie Faye Gates.
claims.notes: Video not watched; description only. Perryman photo rights not verified — cited as link, not downloaded.

claims.claim: A 2022 Pew survey found 36% of Black adults used two or more methods to research family history; 76% of surveyed genealogy researchers relied partly on oral history. (Genealogy context, not reunion-specific.)
claims.source: Smithsonian Magazine, 'How the Smithsonian Is Helping Black Americans Trace Their Roots' (2024), reporting Pew
claims.evidence: Article reports the Pew figures and profiles one family with annual reunions spanning 50+ years and lineage research to the 1700s.
claims.notes: Context only: the survey measures genealogy, not reunion function.

claims.claim: At least one documented family has held annual reunions for more than half a century with lineage research extending to the 1700s.
claims.source: Smithsonian Magazine (2024)
claims.evidence: Single-family profile within the genealogy article.
claims.notes: Single case; illustrates the archive function at its most developed, not the typical reunion.

claims.claim: Reunions function as mutual-aid nodes beyond scholarships (e.g., family associations offering loans and advice; 'reclamation' committees).
claims.source: Ebony planning article (1993)
claims.evidence: Article describes family associations/corporations offering loans, advice, and scholarships, and lists a 'reclamation' committee among standing committees.
claims.notes: Thin evidence: one advice article. Do not generalize 'mutual aid' as a verified universal reunion function.

claims.claim: National prevalence and frequency of Black family reunions (what share of families hold them; how often).
claims.source: None located
claims.evidence: No representative survey of reunion prevalence located in this research pass.
claims.notes: Gap flagged; case studies and journalism cannot substitute for prevalence data.

claims.claim: Reunions measurably improve health, well-being, or other life outcomes for attendees.
claims.source: None located
claims.evidence: No outcome studies located; Vargus's work addresses bonds/identity qualitatively, not measured outcomes.
claims.notes: Do not claim healing/resilience outcomes beyond what case evidence supports.

claims.claim: Black family reunions originated directly from post-emancipation 'Information Wanted' reunification efforts.
claims.source: Only an unverified YouTube video description ('Black family reunions,' Aggressive Intelligence channel)
claims.source_type: Excluded: unverified channel, possible AI narration, no provenance
claims.evidence: No archival or scholarly source located in this pass connecting Information Wanted ads to the reunion institution.
claims.notes: Excluded from the brief as evidence per source standards; noted here to prevent silent use.

claims.claim: Reunion planning advice literature with Chicago-area examples dates to at least 1993 (Lansing, IL host family; Chicago writer Dee Parmer Woodtoor).
claims.source: Ebony planning article (1993)
claims.evidence: Article names a Chicago-area host example in Lansing, Illinois, and quotes Chicago writer Dee Parmer Woodtoor on holding reunions where the family originated.
claims.notes: Documents Chicago-area participation in the reunion-planning discourse, not Chicago-to-South travel.

claims.claim: Reunions have a digital layer: families use websites, Facebook groups, and Ancestry.com for planning and research.
claims.source: Allen dissertation (2020) topic via lauralallen.com; Allen Family Reunion minutes (2016) reference Ancestry research
claims.evidence: Dissertation title confirms online/offline rhetorical practices as the research subject; 2016 minutes document Ancestry.com use in family-history work.
claims.notes: PROVISIONAL pending full-text review of Allen (2022).

claims.claim: Vargus treated the reunion as an independently Black-controlled institution and followed migration routes (north to Boston, south to the Carolinas) in her fieldwork.
claims.source: Temple University memorial (2026)
claims.evidence: Memorial describes her migration-route fieldwork and her framing of the reunion as an independently controlled institution.
claims.notes: Memorial framing; the institutional-autonomy thesis is attributed, not independently tested here.

claims.claim: Boundary definition: a family reunion is a kin-governed recurring gathering; a church homecoming is congregation-governed; a class reunion is cohort-governed; the NCNW Black Family Reunion Celebration is an organization-sponsored public festival.
claims.source: Analytic definition grounded in Jones (1980), AAIHS/Congressional Record (NCNW), and the brief's source base
claims.evidence: Governance criterion distinguishes each form across the source base; each component is independently sourced (C008/C017/C019).
claims.contradictory_evidence: None located; some events blend forms (noted as boundary cases).
claims.notes: This is the brief's own definitional framework, built from sourced components.

claims.claim: COVID-19 moved Black family reunions online.
claims.source: None located for kin reunions (NCNW's 2020 largely-online celebration is a public festival, not a family reunion)
claims.evidence: No evidence located on pandemic-era adaptation of kin-governed reunions.
claims.notes: Do not extrapolate from the NCNW festival's 2020 online format.

claims.claim: Scholarly attention to Black family reunions spans anthropology (Jones 1980), sociology (Vargus 1986-2020), ritual/folklore studies (Auslander 2001), nonprofit/legal studies (Copeland 2018), and technical communication (Allen 2022).
claims.source: Bibliographic verification across journal/publisher/author pages
claims.evidence: Each work's existence, date, and disciplinary home verified via DOI/journal/author/institutional pages.
claims.notes: Maps the field; not a claim about reunion function.
